question: What is the software development life cycle (SDLC)?
correct: The stages a software project moves through, from requirements to maintenance
incorrect: The total amount of time it takes a single program to finish running once
The complete set of git commands a team uses to save and share a project
The list of every programming language the members of a team already know
feedback: The SDLC describes the stages a project moves through: requirements, design, build, test, deploy, and maintain.

question: Why do software teams plan before they start typing code?
correct: Catching a problem early in a requirement is far cheaper than fixing it after release
incorrect: Writing code first is forbidden by most programming languages
Planning makes the finished program run noticeably faster
Typing code early uses up a project's storage space
feedback: A flaw caught in a requirement costs little to fix; the same flaw caught after deployment can be very expensive, so teams plan first.

question: What is the difference between waterfall and agile development?
correct: Waterfall finishes each stage in one long pass; agile works in many short feedback loops
incorrect: Waterfall uses git while agile avoids version control entirely
Waterfall is for small teams while agile is for solo coders
Waterfall writes tests while agile skips testing completely
feedback: Waterfall runs the SDLC as a single long pass with feedback only at the end. Agile runs many short loops, shipping a small slice and adjusting each time.

question: What is a sprint in agile development?
correct: One short cycle, commonly one to four weeks, ending with working software
incorrect: A final stage at the very end where the whole project is deployed all at once
A long meeting in which the entire project design is locked in permanently
A single large git commit that finishes off an entire feature in one step
feedback: A sprint is one short agile cycle (often 1-4 weeks) that ends with a working slice of software and feedback from users.

question: Which of the following are stages of the SDLC? (Select all that apply)
correct: Requirements
Design
Test
Deploy
incorrect: Compile
Refactor
feedback: The SDLC stages are requirements, design, build, test, deploy, and maintain. Compiling and refactoring are activities, not stages of the life cycle.

question: Match each SDLC stage to what happens in it.

pairs.definition: Decide what the software must do
Plan how the software will be built
Check that the software works correctly
Fix and update the software after release

feedback: Each SDLC stage has a clear job, and moving through them in order keeps a project from skipping vital steps.

question: What is a requirement in software engineering?
correct: A precise, testable statement of what the software must do
incorrect: A rough wish about what the software might include
A git command that records a change to the project
A measure of how fast the finished program runs
feedback: A good requirement is precise and testable, so you can later check objectively whether the software meets it.

question: Which of these is written in the correct user-story format?
correct: As a student, I want to reset my password, so that I can log in again
incorrect: The login page should probably be more secure somehow
Add password stuff to the account settings screen
Users sometimes forget passwords and get frustrated
feedback: A user story follows 'As a [role], I want [goal], so that [reason].' It captures who needs the feature and why.

question: A user story is best described as a requirement written from whose point of view?
correct: The user's, stating what they want and why
incorrect: The compiler's, stating how to translate the code
The manager's, stating how long the work will take
The computer's, stating how much memory is needed
feedback: A user story frames a requirement from the user's perspective: as a role, I want a goal, so that I get a benefit.

question: What is version control?
correct: A system that records the full history of changes to a project
incorrect: A tool that automatically writes code for a project
A way to make a program run on older computers
A method for compressing files to save disk space
feedback: Version control keeps the complete history of a project, so teams can collaborate, work in parallel, and recover earlier versions.

question: What is a commit in git?
correct: A saved snapshot of the project, with a message describing the change
incorrect: A request to merge one branch into another one
A separate timeline for building a new change
A teammate's review of proposed changes
feedback: A commit records a snapshot of the project at a point in time, paired with a message that explains what changed and why.

question: What is the staging area in git?
correct: The holding zone for changes you have chosen to include in the next commit
incorrect: The shared website where the whole project is hosted and reviewed online
The separate parallel timeline on which a new feature is gradually built
The complete history log of every past commit ever made in the project
feedback: git add moves changes into the staging area, the holding zone for what will go into your next commit.

question: What is a branch in git?
correct: A separate timeline for building a change without affecting the main version
incorrect: A saved snapshot of the project at one moment
A message that describes what a commit changed
A copy of the project stored on a teammate's laptop
feedback: A branch is an independent line of work. You can build and experiment on it without disturbing the main version until you are ready to merge.

question: In git, a saved snapshot of the project with a description of the change is called a ___.
correct: commit
feedback: A commit is one snapshot in the project's history, created with git commit and labeled by its message.

question: Write the git command that shows the current state of the working tree (which files have changed).
correct: git status
feedback: git status shows which files are modified, staged, or untracked.

question: Write the git command that shows the project's commit history.
correct: git log
feedback: git log lists past commits, newest first, with their messages and authors.

question: Match each git term to its meaning.

pairs.definition: A project tracked by git, with its full history
A saved snapshot with a description
A separate timeline for a change
The holding zone for the next commit

feedback: These four git ideas work together: a repository holds the history, commits are its snapshots, branches let work happen in parallel, and the staging area builds each commit.

question: What is GitHub?
correct: A website that hosts a shared copy of a git project where teams collaborate
incorrect: The version-control tool that git commands run on
A programming language used to build websites
A local folder on your computer holding one commit
feedback: Git is the version-control tool; GitHub is a website that hosts the shared project and is where teams collaborate and review code.

question: What is a pull request (PR)?
correct: A proposal to merge a branch's changes, used to request review
incorrect: A command that downloads the latest code to your laptop
A snapshot of the project saved with a message
A test that checks whether the code is correct
feedback: A pull request proposes merging a branch into the main version and gives teammates a place to review the changes first.

question: What is the purpose of code review?
correct: A teammate reads proposed changes before they are merged
incorrect: A program measures how fast the new code runs
A tool reformats the code to a consistent style
A user tries the finished feature after release
feedback: Code review is a teammate reading proposed changes before they ship. It is a safety net that catches bugs and design problems early.

question: Which of the following are reasons teams use version control and pull requests? (Select all that apply)
correct: To collaborate and work in parallel on the same project
To recover an earlier version when something breaks
To review proposed changes before they are merged
incorrect: To make the finished program run faster for users
To remove the need for any testing of the code
feedback: Version control supports collaboration, recovery, and an audit trail, and pull requests add review before merging. They do not speed up the program or replace testing.

question: What is the key difference between code that runs and code that is correct?
correct: Code can run without errors yet still produce the wrong answer
incorrect: Code that runs is always correct by definition
Correct code is simply code with no comments left in it
Code that runs uses less memory than correct code
feedback: A program can run cleanly and still give a wrong result. Tests are what check correctness, not just whether the code runs.

question: What does an  assert  statement do?
correct: Raises an error if a condition that should be true turns out to be false
incorrect: Prints the value of a variable to the screen
Repeats a block of code until a condition holds
Saves the current state of the project to git
feedback: assert checks a condition you expect to be true. If it is false, Python raises an error, turning a silent bug into a loud failure.

question: Write an assert statement that checks the variable x equals 5.
correct: assert x == 5
feedback: assert x == 5 raises an AssertionError if x is not 5.

question: The Python keyword that raises an error when a condition that should be true is false is ___.
correct: assert
feedback: assert turns a wrong assumption into a loud failure, which is the basis of simple tests.

question: What is a regression?
correct: Working code that breaks because of a later change
incorrect: A feature that was planned but never built
A commit that has not yet been reviewed
A program that runs slower on older hardware
feedback: A regression is when something that used to work breaks after a later change. A saved test catches the regression the moment it happens.

question: Why are tests especially valuable over the long life of a project?
correct: They keep catching regressions every time the code changes later
incorrect: They make the program run faster for every user
They remove the need to write clear requirements
They let the team skip code review before merging
feedback: Tests guard against regressions forever after: each later change is re-checked automatically, so a newly introduced break shows up loudly.

question: In 2026, when AI drafts much of the code, what does the AI actually produce?
correct: Plausible output that may be correct, not guaranteed-correct output
incorrect: Output that is proven correct before you see it
Output that has already been tested on real users
Output that can never contain a security flaw
feedback: An AI assistant generates plausible code, not guaranteed-correct code. The human engineering around it, including testing and review, is what makes it trustworthy.

question: What is a hallucination in the context of AI-generated code?
correct: Confident output that is wrong or invented, such as a nonexistent function
incorrect: A deliberate bug that the AI knowingly hides somewhere inside the code
A helpful comment the AI adds in order to explain its own reasoning
A test the AI writes on its own to check whether its output is correct
feedback: A hallucination is confident but false AI output, like calling a function that does not exist. It is why you verify AI code instead of trusting it.

question: In AI-assisted development, what is the spec, and why does it matter?
correct: The precise description of what to build, which the human authors and keeps
incorrect: The compiled, machine-code version of the program the AI just produced
The git branch on which the AI's generated code happens to be stored
The raw speed at which the AI is able to generate its code output
feedback: The spec is the precise description of what to build. In AI-assisted work it is the real artifact the human owns, while the generated code is downstream of it.

question: What is decomposition, and whose job is it in AI-assisted work?
correct: Breaking a problem into well-defined pieces; it is the engineer's job, not the AI's
incorrect: Deleting old commits from the project; the AI's job
Translating code into machine code; the compiler's job
Reviewing a pull request; the project manager's job
feedback: Decomposition means deciding what functions should exist and how the problem breaks apart. That judgment is the engineer's responsibility, even when AI writes the code.

question: What does iterative development with an AI assistant look like?
correct: Treating the AI's output as a first draft and refining it through review
incorrect: Accepting the AI's first output and shipping it at once
Asking the AI the same question until it gives up
Writing all the code by hand and ignoring the AI
feedback: Iterative development treats AI output as a first draft: you review it, test it, and refine it in a loop rather than trusting the first attempt.

question: What does accountability mean in AI-assisted software development?
correct: A responsible human owns the code, even when an AI drafted it
incorrect: The AI is blamed for any bugs that reach users
No one is responsible once the code is merged
The fastest coder on the team takes the blame
feedback: Accountability means a responsible person owns the code regardless of who or what wrote it. Some flaws, like a privacy violation, only a human can be answerable for.

question: Which of the following are good practices when reviewing AI-generated code? (Select all that apply)
correct: Run tests you wrote yourself against the code
Check that called functions and methods actually exist
Judge whether the code meets the real requirement
incorrect: Merge it immediately because the AI sounds confident
Assume any code that runs is therefore correct
feedback: Reviewing AI code means testing it, checking for hallucinated functions, and judging it against the requirement. Confidence and 'it runs' are not evidence of correctness.

question: Match each AI-assisted development term to its meaning.

pairs.definition: The precise description of what to build
Confident AI output that is wrong or invented
Working code that a later change breaks
A human owning the code an AI drafted

feedback: As AI writes more code, these human-centered ideas, authoring the spec, catching hallucinations and regressions, and owning the result, matter more, not less.

question: The instructions you give an AI assistant, which act as a kind of spec, are called the ___.
correct: prompt
feedback: A prompt is the instruction given to an AI assistant. A clear prompt is effectively a spec for what you want built.

question: An agile team runs sprints of {{len}} weeks each. How many full sprints fit in a {{weeks}}-week schedule?
feedback_template: Each sprint is {{len}} weeks, so {{weeks}} weeks holds floor({{weeks}} / {{len}}) = {{expected}} full sprints.

question: A function add(a, b) is supposed to return a + b. A test runs assert add({{a}}, {{b}}) == ?. What value should replace the ? so the test passes?
feedback_template: A correct add returns {{a}} + {{b}} = {{expected}}, so the test should assert the result equals {{expected}}.
